concerns.text: The validation design is circular/tautological. FR-004 and SC-001 require validating the 'optimized ratio' by comparing it to the '1:1 baseline' using ANOVA. However, the 'optimized ratio' is DEFINED as the ratio that maximizes yield in the simulation (US-1). By definition, the maximum of a set is greater than or equal to any other specific member of that set (including 1:1). Testing if Max(Y) > Y(1:1) is a mathematical identity, not an empirical finding. The p-value will be < 0.05 by construction unless the simulation is broken, rendering the statistical test meaningless for validating the research hypothesis.

The claim of 'non-linearity' (SC-002) is being validated against a 'flat or linear trend' hypothesis, but the spec does not define a null model for the relationship between latitude and optimal ratio. Without a theoretical baseline (e.g., 'optimal ratio is constant regardless of latitude'), the observation of a curve is merely a description of the data, not a validation of a specific scientific mechanism. The spec treats the existence of a curve as a 'finding' rather than an inevitable consequence of varying solar spectra/angles with latitude.

The computational constraint (6 CPU-hours on 2 CPU) for a 10-year hourly simulation (87,600 hours) across 20 locations and 500 ratios (876 million time-step evaluations) is likely physically impossible for a physics-based model including electrolyzer efficiency curves and startup thresholds. This is a category error in resource estimation that will force the model to be oversimplified (e.g., using annual averages instead of hourly data), which would invalidate the core physics of the 'mismatch' problem the research aims to solve.
